theme: The forerunner; the sun of righteousness, silence before the Word
readingInstruction: Read Malachi 3:1-4:6. The messenger will prepare the way, the LORD will suddenly come to his temple, and the book ends with the promise of Elijah. This is the last page of the Old Testament in the Christian canon. Read it slowly, as the lights go down.
settingTheScene: Malachi’s last two chapters answer the people’s question, “Where is the God of justice?” God says he is coming. But first a messenger will prepare the way. Then, the LORD himself will come to his temple. The book also addresses the question of tithing, and distinguishes those who serve God from those who do not. It ends with a promise and a warning. After this, there are about four hundred years of silence before the word of God comes again.
observation: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me” (3:1).
“And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming” (3:1).
“But who can endure the day of his coming?… For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers” soap’ (3:2).
“For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed” (3:6).
“Return to me, and I will return to you” (3:7).
“Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house” (3:10).
“But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings” (4:2).

“Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers” (4:5-6).
interpretation:
The key announcement is in 3:1. A messenger will prepare the way, and then “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.” The people were asking, “Where is the God of justice?” God says, “I am coming.” But the coming will not be what they expect. They wanted judgment on their enemies. But the LORD says that he will first purify his own people. “Who can endure the day of his coming?” He is like a refiner’s fire and fullers’ soap. He will purify the sons of Levi until they present right offerings.

The next section is a call to return, based on God’s unchanging character: “I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed.” This is one of the great verses of grace. The reason Israel survives is not their faithfulness but God’s. “Return to me, and I will return to you.” The people then ask, “How shall we return?” God says they have robbed him in tithes and offerings. He invites them to bring the full tithe and “put me to the test,” with the promise that he will open the windows of heaven. The test is about trust, not a formula for wealth.

Then there is a division. The people had said that it is vain to serve God. But a group “who feared the LORD spoke with one another,” and the LORD listened and wrote a book of remembrance. “They shall be mine… in the day when I make up my treasured possession.” God keeps a record of the faithful.

The last chapter describes the day coming, burning like an oven, when the proud will be stubble. But for those who fear his name, “the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings.” That is one of the most beautiful images in the Old Testament. The book ends with a command to remember the law of Moses, and a promise of Elijah to turn hearts before the great day.

Then there is silence. For four hundred years, no prophet speaks. But the promise is hanging in the air: a messenger, a coming Lord, a rising sun.
connection: Mark 1:2-4 and Matthew 11:10-14 identify John the Baptist as the messenger and as Elijah. Luke 1:17 says John would go before him “in the spirit and power of Elijah.” Luke 1:78-79: “The sunrise shall visit us from on high.” John 2:13-22: Jesus comes to the temple. Hebrews 13:8: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” Revelation 20:12 mentions the books that are opened. Matthew 3:1-3 introduces John the Baptist.
application:
Read Mark 1:1-8 immediately after this passage. Notice where the Old Testament ends and the Gospel begins.

Give to God first, and trust him to provide.

Pray for the “turning of hearts” between fathers and children in your family.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he does not change and so you are not consumed.
Ask him to refine you and return you to him.
Ask him to prepare you for the coming of the Lord.
